title: Free fall and geodesics
one_line_summary: Defines geodesics as the stationary-interval paths that free particles follow, explains when such paths are minima, saddles or maxima (conjugate points, and the Lorentzian maximum of proper time), finds them by variational calculus with length parametrization, recasts them as curves that parallel transport their own tangent to get the component geodesic equation, reinterprets the connection term as an inertial force (gravity included), and treats light with the null condition, ending in the Shapiro time delay.
role_in_book: Second chapter of Part II. Chapter 6 argued that free fall is the natural state and gravity is locally removable, and Chapter 7 built parallel transport, connection coefficients and the covariant derivative. This chapter joins the two: the free-fall world line is a geodesic, and the geodesic equation is the relativistic replacement for Newton's second law with no force. It deliberately stops short of a systematic way to compute connection coefficients (that is Chapter 9, which also rederives the geodesic equation from an action) and of curvature proper (Chapter 11, where geodesic deviation becomes the test for true curvature). Its conjugate-point remark seeds the singularity theorem of Chapter 50, its null-geodesic and weak-field material is reused in Chapters 14, 23 and 24, and the geodesic equation with a force term becomes the workhorse of the orbit chapters in Part IV.

Calculus of variations and the chain rule for reparametrized integrals
Line element ds^2 = g_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu, metric signature and the sign of timelike, null and spacelike intervals
Light cones and the coordinate speed of light read off from ds^2 = 0
Parallel transport, connection coefficients and the covariant derivative along a curve (nabla_u v)
Connection coefficients of plane polar coordinates (Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r, Gamma^theta_{r theta} = 1/r)
Equivalence principle, local flatness and local inertial frames
Weak-field line element with g_tt = -(1 + 2 Phi)
4-velocity, 4-momentum, proper time and the normalization u.u = -1
Newtonian gravitational potential Phi = -GM/r and force = -m grad Phi
Circular motion, centripetal force, and centrifugal and Coriolis forces in rotating frames
Principle of general covariance: a tensor equation true in one frame holds in all

learning_objectives: Reader can state the geodesic principle (free massive particles follow timelike geodesics, light follows null geodesics) and explain why a particle acted on by other interactions does not.

Reader can explain why a stationary path need not be a minimum, using the sphere example of the short arc versus the long arc through the antipode, and define a conjugate point as a focus of neighbouring geodesics.
Reader can argue with the null zigzag construction that proper time along timelike curves has no positive lower bound, so a timelike geodesic is (locally) a curve of maximum proper time.
Reader can set up the length functional s = integral of L d lambda for a given metric and write the Euler-Lagrange equations for its coordinates.
Reader can show that the length functional is unchanged by reparametrization and use length parametrization (L = 1) after taking the first derivatives, keeping L = 1 as an extra first integral.
Reader can derive geodesic equations for the plane (Cartesian and polar) and the unit sphere, and check which trial curves (meridians, the equator, a latitude circle) satisfy them.
Reader can define a geodesic geometrically as a curve that parallel transports its own tangent vector and expand nabla_u u = 0 into the component geodesic equation.
Reader can prove that u.u is constant along an affinely parametrized geodesic, so the causal character of a geodesic never changes.
Reader can justify nabla_p p = 0 by writing momentum conservation in a local inertial frame and promoting it with general covariance.

Reader can identify -m Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} xdot^alpha xdot^beta as an inertial force, reproduce centrifugal and Coriolis-type terms from plane-polar connection coefficients, and add an external 4-force to the geodesic equation.
Reader can extract Newtonian gravity from the weak-field metric via Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi and explain in what sense gravity is an inertial force.

Reader can use the null condition ds^2 = 0 with the weak-field metric including the spatial correction to compute the Shapiro time delay 2GM ln(4 d_p d_e / b^2) and estimate its size for a solar-conjunction radar signal.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, variational-first chapter. It opens by asserting the physical claim (free fall is geodesic motion) and justifying it in a margin note via the point-particle action, then spends most of its length on what 'extremal' really means and on the mechanics of finding geodesics by the Euler-Lagrange route, before switching to the geometric definition (self-parallel tangent) to get the general component equation. Nearly every idea is carried by an Example block: straight lines in the plane, great circles on the sphere, swingball, the weak-field Newtonian limit, polar-coordinate mechanics, and the Shapiro delay. The sphere is the recurring model space, and inertial forces from everyday rotating frames are the bridge to the claim that gravity is a connection effect. Several subtle points (conjugate points, the second variation, affine parameters, the weak-field spatial metric) are deliberately flagged and deferred to Chapters 9, 14, 45 and 50.
narrative_arc: Claim up front: geodesics are straightest paths and extremize the interval; freely falling particles follow them (margin justification from the action S = -m integral dtau).
Anchor in flat spacetime: zero acceleration gives straight world lines x^mu = b^mu tau + c^mu.
Question the word 'extremal': Hamilton's principle only needs a stationary action, and minima, saddles and maxima all occur.

Sphere model: two geodesics on one great circle between q1 and q2; the one passing the antipode is a saddle, diagnosed by launching a swarm of particles and watching it refocus at the conjugate point.

Signature decides the character: Riemannian lengths have a floor (minimum), Lorentzian proper times have no floor, shown by approximating any timelike curve by null zigzags, so timelike geodesics maximize proper time.
Formalism: write the interval as an action with L = |(ds/dlambda)^2|^(1/2) and apply Euler-Lagrange.

Detour on parametrization: prove the length is reparametrization invariant, then take derivatives first and only afterwards fix lambda = s so that L = 1, which is both a simplification and a constraint.
Check on the plane: second derivatives of x and y vanish, reproducing straight lines.
Model space: derive the two sphere equations, verify meridians and the equator as solutions and reject a latitude circle.
Geometric reformulation: free fall means zero covariant acceleration, a geodesic parallel transports its own tangent, and expanding nabla_u u = 0 gives the component geodesic equation.
Consequences: u.u is conserved so causal type is fixed; affine parameters defined as those that keep the equation in this form; photons have no proper time.
Momentum version nabla_p p = 0 via local inertial frame plus general covariance.
Reinterpretation: the connection term acts like an inertial force; swingball two-frame free-body diagram as the familiar case; equivalence principle turns gravity into such a force.
Check against Newton: weak-field metric gives Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi, the Newtonian gravitational acceleration.

Add real forces: geodesic equation with a 4-force on the right; application to polar-coordinate mechanics showing centrifugal and Coriolis-like terms, and that circular motion needs a centripetal force.
Light: null geodesics with tangent light cones; shortcut ds^2 = 0 applied to the improved weak-field metric gives the coordinate speed of light.
Application: integrate the delay along a straight path past the Sun to get the logarithmic Shapiro delay, framed as the fourth classical test.

Summary equation m(xddot + Gamma xdot xdot) = f unifies geometry, inertial forces and external forces; exercises revisit polar straight lines and derive the geodesic equation from a freely falling frame.
signature_moves: Diagnosing minimum versus saddle by a physical thought experiment (a spray of particles on a sphere refocusing at the antipode) instead of computing the second variation.
The null zigzag picture: a timelike curve is arbitrarily close to a chain of zero-length light-like segments, which instantly shows proper time has no positive minimum.

Two-stage use of the parametrization freedom: differentiate the Lagrangian with lambda unspecified, then set lambda = s so the square root disappears, with an explicit warning that this is not 'varying the number 1'.
Testing candidate curves on the sphere against the derived equations, including a deliberate non-solution (a latitude circle) so learners see the equation discriminating.
Deriving the component geodesic equation not from the action but from 'zero covariant acceleration', making the geodesic the curved-space analogue of xddot = 0.

Treating the connection term uniformly as an inertial force, then using a playground game (swingball/tetherball) and polar-coordinate Newtonian mechanics to make that reading concrete before applying it to gravity.
Reading connection coefficients off an equation of motion (Example 8.10) rather than computing them from the formula, previewing the Chapter 9 method.
Avoiding the full null geodesic equation for light: impose ds^2 = 0 directly and integrate, reaching a real observable (Shapiro delay) in a few lines.
Short proofs by the local-inertial-frame-plus-covariance argument (momentum conservation) and by metric compatibility (constancy of u.u).

sections.title: Chapter opening: geodesics and the flat-spacetime baseline
sections.summary: States the chapter's thesis that geodesics are the straightest paths of a curved spacetime, extremize the interval, and are the world lines of freely falling bodies, with the geodesic equation playing the role of a force-free equation of motion. A margin note justifies free fall along geodesics from the point-particle action proportional to proper time, stresses that only free particles do this, and introduces spacelike and null geodesics. Example 8.1 recovers straight world lines in Minkowski spacetime.
concepts: action for a free relativistic particle
key_moves: Assert the geometric (straightest path) and variational (extremal interval) characterizations of a geodesic together.
Justify geodesic motion from S = -m integral (-ds^2)^(1/2): since m is a constant, extremizing S extremizes proper time.
Warn that interactions add terms to the Lagrangian, so charged or pushed particles do not follow geodesics.
In flat spacetime set d^2x^mu/dtau^2 = 0 and integrate to straight lines x^mu = b^mu tau + c^mu.

sections.title: Extremal intervals
sections.summary: Points out that Hamilton's principle only requires a stationary action, and uses non-relativistic motion on a sphere to show that of two great-circle routes between points the one through the antipode is a saddle, detected by the refocusing of a swarm of nearby trajectories at a conjugate point (with a pointer to the singularity theorems). Then compares metrics: in a positive-definite metric path length is bounded below, so geodesics are locally shortest; in a Lorentzian metric proper time along timelike curves can be made arbitrarily small by null zigzags, so a timelike geodesic, if extremal, maximizes proper time.
concepts: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve
key_moves: Distinguish stationary from minimal action and say saddles and maxima matter in relativity.
Sphere example: short arc (i) is a minimum of the action; long arc (ii) through the antipode is a saddle.
Launch a fan of particles with slightly different momenta; linear response delta q^i = N_ij delta p^j; on the sphere all refocus at the antipode q1*, the conjugate point.
Rule from the margin: a geodesic that passes a conjugate point is not a minimum.
Signature ++++: lengths bounded below, geodesic locally shortest (but a given geodesic need not be the shortest route).
Signature -+++: timelike curves approximated by chains of null segments have arbitrarily small proper time, so the extremum is a maximum.

sections.title: Length parametrization and first geodesic calculations (plane and sphere, continuing §8.1)
sections.summary: Writes the interval as an action with Lagrangian L = |(ds/dlambda)^2|^(1/2), applies it to the Euclidean plane, and pauses to show that the length is invariant under any reparametrization. The recipe is to take the partial derivatives of L with the parameter unspecified and only then choose lambda equal to arc length (proper time or proper length), which sets L = 1 and supplies a redundant but useful constraint. The plane then yields vanishing second derivatives (straight lines), and the unit sphere yields a theta equation with a sin theta cos theta phidot^2 term and a conserved sin^2 theta phidot, solved by meridians and the equator but not by a latitude circle at theta = pi/4.
concepts: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional
reparametrization invariance of the length functional
straight lines as geodesics of flat space
great circles as geodesics of the sphere
key_moves: Identify L(x, xdot) = |(ds/dlambda)^2|^(1/2) so that s = integral L d lambda.
Chain-rule proof that s has the same form in any parameter eta (margin eqns 8.7-8.8).
Differentiate L first (partial L / partial xdot = xdot / L), then choose d lambda = ds so L = 1; the parameter then physically measures proper time or proper length.
Plane: d^2x/dlambda^2 = d^2y/dlambda^2 = 0; verify with x = lambda, y = m lambda + c.
Sphere: derive (8.19) and (8.20); the latter expands to (8.18) with a 2 cot theta thetadot phidot term.
Test trial curves: theta = lambda, phi = 0 works; theta = pi/2, phi = lambda works; theta = pi/4, phi = lambda fails because sin theta cos theta is not zero there.

sections.title: A geodesic equation
sections.summary: Defines the covariant acceleration a = Du/dtau = nabla_u u and argues that a freely falling particle, feeling no force, has a = 0, so a geodesic is a curve that parallel transports its own tangent vector, a definition that works for any causal type and any affine parameter. Expanding with connection coefficients gives the component geodesic equation. Margin notes define affine parameters as those related to proper time linearly and preserving this form, and note photons have no proper time. Example 8.7 shows u.u is conserved along a geodesic, and Example 8.8 establishes nabla_p p = 0 by a local-inertial-frame argument.
concepts: conservation of u.u along a geodesic
key_moves: Free fall means no force, hence zero covariant acceleration Du/dtau = 0.
Recognize nabla_u u = 0 as parallel transport of the tangent along itself.
Components: u^alpha(partial_alpha u^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^beta) = 0.
Use u^alpha partial_alpha u^mu = du^mu/dlambda = d^2x^mu/dlambda^2 to reach (8.24).
Affine parameters: lambda = a tau + b; null curves use an affine parameter sigma with g_{mu nu} x'^mu x'^nu = 0.
Leibniz rule: nabla_u(u.u) = 2 u.nabla_u u = 0, so timelike stays timelike, null stays null.
In a LIF Gamma = 0 so dp/dtau = 0 reads nabla_p p = 0, a tensor equation that therefore holds everywhere.

sections.title: Inertial forces
sections.summary: Reads the connection term of the geodesic equation as an inertial force, which can arise from genuine curvature or merely from the coordinates. The swingball (tetherball) example shows how a centripetal tension in the players' frame becomes a balance against a centrifugal force in the ball's frame. Via the equivalence principle gravity is itself such an inertial force; the weak-field metric gives Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi, reproducing Newtonian gravity. An external 4-force is added on the right-hand side, and the result is applied to Newtonian motion in plane polar coordinates, where the connection yields centrifugal and Coriolis-like terms.
concepts: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation
connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates
key_moves: f_inertial^mu = -m Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} xdot^alpha xdot^beta.
Non-zero Gamma can come from curvature or from coordinates alone.
Swingball: T cos theta = mg, T sin theta = mv^2/r in the lab; in the ball's frame an outward force F balances T sin theta.
Equivalence principle: gravitational acceleration of one particle is indistinguishable from a coordinate effect.
Weak field: compare the equation of motion with the geodesic equation and read off Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi = GM x^i / r^3.
Add f^mu: m(xddot^mu + Gamma xdot xdot) = f^mu.
Polar coordinates: f^r/m = rddot - r thetadot^2 and f^theta/m = thetaddot + 2 rdot thetadot / r; uniform circular motion needs an inward f^r.

sections.title: Geodesics for photons
sections.summary: Light follows null geodesics, with the light cone tangent to the world line at every point. Rather than solve the null geodesic equation, the authors impose ds^2 = 0 on the weak-field metric that includes the spatial factor (1 - 2 Phi), obtain the coordinate speed of light, and integrate along a straight path grazing the Sun to derive the Shapiro time delay, logarithmic in the impact parameter. A margin note places Shapiro's proposal as the fourth solar-system test after perihelion precession, light bending and gravitational redshift.
concepts: null condition method for light rays
weak-field metric with spatial curvature term
classical solar-system tests of general relativity
key_moves: Photons are massless and free, so they follow null geodesics; free massive particles follow timelike ones.
Use ds^2 = 0 directly instead of the geodesic equation.
Quote the improved weak-field metric (8.37) with both g_tt and g_ij perturbed (derivation deferred to §14.1 and Chapter 45).
Obtain dt/dx ≈ 1 + 2GM/r to first order in GM/r.
Integrate 2GM/sqrt(x^2 + b^2) using the arcsinh-type integral to get 2GM ln(2|x0|/b) for each leg.
Add the two legs to get Delta t = 2GM ln(4 d_p d_e / b^2).

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Recaps three points: geodesics are free-fall paths found by extremizing the interval with length parametrization easing the work, with massive particles on timelike geodesics; the equation of motion with connection and force terms ties acceleration to geometry and to applied forces, the connection part giving inertial forces; and light travels on null geodesics, handled most easily through ds^2 = 0.
key_moves: State the master equation (8.42) and note f^mu = 0 recovers the geodesic equation.

concepts.name: geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve in a space or spacetime that is as straight as the geometry allows: equivalently, an affinely parametrized curve whose tangent is parallel transported along itself, and (locally) a curve that makes the interval between its endpoints stationary.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced in the opening paragraph with both the straightness and the extremal-interval descriptions, then made computable first by the variational route (§8.1) and later by the parallel-transport route (§8.2).

concepts.name: geodesic principle
concepts.definition: The physical postulate that a massive particle subject to no non-gravitational interaction moves on a timelike geodesic of spacetime, while light moves on a null geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a physical fact in the opening and supported in a margin note: the free-particle action is minus mass times proper time, so its stationary paths are timelike geodesics. Named explicitly in a later margin note that contrasts massive particles with photons.
prerequisites: action for a free relativistic particle
concepts.notes: The book stresses that only free particles obey it; extra interactions add Lagrangian terms and spoil geodesic motion. Strictly, margin note 13 attaches the name 'geodesic principle' to the massive-particle statement only; the null-geodesic rule for light is stated alongside it.

concepts.name: action for a free relativistic particle
concepts.definition: For a free particle of mass m the action is S = -m times the integral of (-ds^2)^(1/2) along the world line, i.e. -m times the elapsed proper time (units with c = 1); stationary S means stationary proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from mechanics in the first margin note as the justification for the geodesic principle.
concepts.notes: Chapter 9 §9.2 returns to deriving the geodesic equation from an action.

concepts.name: stationary action
concepts.definition: The trajectory a system actually follows is one for which the first-order variation of the action vanishes; this can be a minimum, a saddle point or a maximum of the action, not necessarily a minimum.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens §8.1 as a correction to the habit of saying 'least action', motivating why relativity needs maxima (proper time) and saddles (paths through conjugate points).
prerequisites: Lagrangian mechanics and the Euler-Lagrange equations (GA ch2)

concepts.name: conjugate point
concepts.definition: A point Q on a geodesic from P at which geodesics leaving P in infinitesimally different directions reconverge; there the map from initial momentum (direction) perturbations to final position perturbations is singular. A geodesic segment containing a point conjugate to its start is no longer a local minimum of length (for Riemannian metrics) or a local maximum of proper time (for timelike curves).
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.2: particles launched from q1 on a sphere with slightly different directions spread out and then all meet at the antipode q1*. A margin note gives the general criterion via the matrix N_ij in delta q^i = N_ij delta p^j and flags its use in singularity theorems.
prerequisites: great circles as geodesics of the sphere
concepts.notes: The margin note says N^{-1} is singular; strictly N becomes singular (has a zero eigenvalue) and N^{-1} fails to exist. Developed properly in Chapter 50.

concepts.name: Riemannian metric
concepts.definition: A metric for which every non-zero displacement has positive squared length; lengths of curves between two points are then bounded below, so geodesics are locally length-minimizing.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.3 contrasts it with the Lorentzian case to show the signature determines whether geodesics minimize or maximize.
concepts.notes: The reading copy garbles the signatures in Example 8.3; the printed page shows ++++ for Riemannian and -+++ for Lorentzian.

concepts.name: Lorentzian metric
concepts.definition: A metric with one negative and three positive eigenvalues (signature -+++ in this book), so intervals are negative for timelike, zero for null and positive for spacelike separations.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.3, as the counterpart of the Riemannian case, leading to the maximum-proper-time property.

concepts.name: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
concepts.definition: Among timelike curves joining two timelike-separated events (and close to the geodesic, absent conjugate points), the timelike geodesic has the greatest proper time; there is no lower bound, since timelike curves can have proper time arbitrarily close to zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.3: stated as the 'wrong way round' result caused by the minus sign in the metric, and supported by the null zigzag construction of Fig. 8.2.
prerequisites: null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve

concepts.name: null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve
concepts.definition: Any smooth timelike curve can be approximated arbitrarily well, as a set of points, by a chain of null segments; each segment has zero interval, so the total proper time of such nearby paths tends to zero, showing proper time is not bounded below.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 8.2 and the end of Example 8.3, used as a graphical sanity check that timelike geodesics cannot be minima.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional
concepts.definition: Treat L(x, xdot) = |g_{mu nu} xdot^mu xdot^nu|^(1/2), with dot = d/dlambda, as a Lagrangian and impose d/dlambda (partial L / partial xdot^mu) = partial L / partial x^mu for each coordinate; the solutions are the geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Eqn 8.3 splits the interval into small pieces to read off L, and the Chapter 2 Euler-Lagrange machinery is applied first to the plane (Example 8.4) and then to the sphere (Example 8.6).
formulas: s = \int \mathrm d\lambda\, L(x^\mu,\dot x^\mu),\quad L = \left|\left(\tfrac{\mathrm ds}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2\right|^{1/2}
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot x^\mu} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x^\mu}

concepts.name: reparametrization invariance of the length functional
concepts.definition: The integral of |ds/dlambda| d lambda has the same form and value in any monotonic parameter eta = eta(lambda), because the factor d lambda/d eta from the measure cancels the factor d eta/d lambda from each velocity inside the square root.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 3 on p.93 carries out the chain rule explicitly for the 2D Cartesian length after the text observes that lambda -> a lambda + b changes nothing.
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional
formulas: \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda} = \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\eta}\frac{\mathrm d\eta}{\mathrm d\lambda},\quad \mathrm d\lambda = \frac{\mathrm d\lambda}{\mathrm d\eta}\mathrm d\eta
concepts.notes: This invariance is why the square-root Lagrangian leaves the parameter undetermined and a gauge choice (length parametrization) is needed.

concepts.name: length parametrization
concepts.definition: Choosing the curve parameter equal to the accumulated interval, d lambda = ds (proper time for timelike curves, proper length for spacelike ones), so that the Lagrangian L equals 1 along the solution; this is done only after the derivatives of L have been taken, and L = 1 then serves as an additional first integral.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the labour-saving choice exploiting the freedom just demonstrated; the text insists it is also needed to interpret the parameter physically and warns that setting L = 1 before varying would be wrong.
prerequisites: reparametrization invariance of the length functional
Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional
concepts.notes: Not available for null curves (ds = 0); there one uses an affine parameter directly (margin note 8).

concepts.name: straight lines as geodesics of flat space
concepts.definition: In flat space, geodesics are straight lines: in Cartesian coordinates every coordinate is linear in the arc-length parameter, and in plane polar coordinates the same line appears as r = a / cos(theta - theta0), with a the perpendicular distance from the origin.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.1 (Minkowski world lines), Examples 8.4-8.5 (Euclidean plane) as the 'we know the answer' check, and Exercises 8.1-8.2 for polar coordinates with Fig. 8.7.
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional

concepts.name: great circles as geodesics of the sphere
concepts.definition: On a sphere of unit radius with metric d theta^2 + sin^2 theta d phi^2, the geodesic equations are thetaddot = sin theta cos theta phidot^2 and d/dlambda(sin^2 theta phidot) = 0; their solutions are arcs of great circles such as meridians and the equator, while circles of latitude other than the equator are not geodesics.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.6 derives the equations with length parametrization; a margin note tests explicit trial curves; Fig. 8.3 shows meridian A and equator B as solutions and latitude circle C as a non-solution. The sphere also serves as the model space for conjugate points in Example 8.2.
prerequisites: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional
concepts.notes: The conserved sin^2 theta phidot is the angular momentum about the polar axis, a point the book does not make here.

concepts.name: covariant acceleration
concepts.definition: The rate of change of the 4-velocity along the world line measured with the covariant derivative, a = Du/dtau = nabla_u u; it is the acceleration an attached accelerometer would register, and it vanishes for free fall.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening line of §8.2: defined and immediately set to zero for a particle that feels no force.
formulas: \mathbf a = \frac{\mathrm D\mathbf u}{\mathrm d\tau} = \nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u

concepts.name: geodesic as autoparallel curve
aliases: curve that parallel transports its own tangent
concepts.definition: Geometric definition of a geodesic: a curve whose tangent vector u satisfies nabla_u u = 0, i.e. the tangent is parallel transported along the curve; it applies to timelike, null and spacelike curves with any affine parameter.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached in §8.2 by combining 'free fall = zero covariant acceleration' with the Chapter 7 definition of parallel transport (nabla_u v = 0).
concepts.notes: Equivalence of this definition with the extremal-interval definition assumes the Levi-Civita (metric-compatible, symmetric) connection; Chapter 9 closes that loop.

concepts.name: geodesic equation
concepts.definition: The second-order ODE d^2x^mu/dlambda^2 + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} (dx^alpha/dlambda)(dx^beta/dlambda) = 0 satisfied by the coordinates of an affinely parametrized geodesic; with lambda = tau it is the equation of motion of a force-free massive particle.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by writing nabla_u u = 0 in components with the Chapter 7 expression for the covariant derivative and replacing u^alpha partial_alpha u^mu by the ordinary derivative along the path.
formulas: \frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm d\lambda} = 0

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic in terms of which the geodesic equation takes its standard form with zero right-hand side; any two are related by lambda -> a lambda + b with constants a, b, and for timelike curves proper time is one of them.
concepts.how_introduced: Used from Example 8.1 onwards; margin note 8 gives the linear relation to tau and the characterization by the form of the geodesic equation, and notes that null curves need one because they have no proper time.
concepts.notes: Characterizing affine parameters by the form of the equation is circular unless one shows what a non-affine parameter adds (a term proportional to the tangent); the book does not show it.

concepts.name: conservation of u.u along a geodesic
aliases: causal character of a geodesic is preserved
concepts.definition: Along an affinely parametrized geodesic the squared norm u.u of the tangent is constant, because its derivative is 2u.nabla_u u = 0; hence a geodesic that starts timelike (u.u = -1), null (0) or spacelike (+1 with proper-length parameter) stays so.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.7, a one-line application of the Leibniz rule to the geometric geodesic equation.
formulas: \nabla_{\mathbf u}(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) = 2\,\mathbf u\cdot(\nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u) = 0
concepts.notes: Silently uses nabla g = 0 so the covariant derivative obeys the product rule through the dot product.

concepts.name: metric compatibility of the connection
concepts.definition: The property that the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes, so parallel transport preserves dot products and the Leibniz rule holds for u.v.
concepts.how_introduced: Not named in this chapter; it is relied on implicitly in Example 8.7. It comes from Chapter 7 §7.5 ('Enter the metric').
formulas:

abla_{\mathbf w}\mathbf u)\cdot\mathbf v + \mathbf u\cdot
