concepts.name: geometric momentum conservation
concepts.definition: For a free particle the 4-momentum is parallel transported along itself, nabla_p p = 0; for massive particles this is m times the geodesic equation, and for photons, whose momentum is tangent to the null world line, it is the null geodesic equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated from nabla_u u = 0 and proved in Example 8.8: in a local inertial frame the connection vanishes so the flat-space law dp/dtau = 0 is nabla_p p = 0, and as a tensor equation it holds in every frame.
formulas: (\nabla_{\mathbf p}\mathbf p)^\beta = m\left(\frac{\mathrm dp^\beta}{\mathrm d\tau} + u^\alpha p^\sigma\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\sigma}\right)

concepts.name: local inertial frame
concepts.definition: Coordinates about a point in which the metric takes the Minkowski form and all connection coefficients vanish at that point, so special-relativistic laws hold there.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in Example 8.8 as the frame in which momentum conservation takes its flat-space form.

concepts.name: principle of general covariance
concepts.definition: A physical law written as a tensor equation that holds in one coordinate system (for instance a local inertial frame) holds in all coordinate systems.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Example 8.8 to lift dp/dtau = 0 from a LIF to nabla_p p = 0 everywhere.

concepts.name: inertial force
concepts.definition: The apparent force m xddot^mu = -m Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} xdot^alpha xdot^beta that a coordinate description attributes to a free particle because the connection coefficients are non-zero; it arises from curvilinear or accelerating coordinates, from genuine curvature, or both.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening of §8.3: moving the connection term of the geodesic equation to the other side and calling it a force; illustrated by the rotating Earth and swingball, and by the centrifugal and Coriolis-like terms in polar coordinates.

concepts.name: centrifugal force
aliases: outward inertial force in a rotating frame
concepts.definition: The outward inertial force of magnitude mv^2/r that appears in a frame co-rotating with a body in circular motion, balancing the inward real force in that frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.9 with swingball: horizontal tension provides the centripetal force in the players' frame; in the ball's frame the same tension is balanced by an outward F.

concepts.name: equivalence principle
concepts.definition: For a single particle, the effects of a gravitational field cannot be distinguished locally from those of an accelerated or curvilinear choice of coordinates; hence gravitational acceleration can be encoded in connection coefficients.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the end of Example 8.9 to conclude that gravity enters the geodesic equation as an inertial force.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation
concepts.definition: For the static weak-field metric ds^2 = -(1 + 2 Phi) dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 and slow motion (tau ≈ t), the spatial geodesic equations reduce to xddot^i = -partial_i Phi because Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi; for Phi = -GM/r this is Newton's inverse-square attraction.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.10: the equation of motion is quoted (method deferred to Chapter 9) and the connection coefficients are read off by comparison with the geodesic equation.
concepts.notes: The book calls these the only non-zero coefficients; Gamma^t_{ti} = partial_i Phi/(1 + 2 Phi) is also non-zero but does not enter the spatial equations.

concepts.name: geodesic equation with an external 4-force
aliases: relativistic Newton's second law in curved spacetime
concepts.definition: When a 4-force f acts, m(d^2x^mu/dtau^2 + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} dx^alpha/dtau dx^beta/dtau) = f^mu; the left side is m times the covariant acceleration, and f^mu = 0 recovers the geodesic equation. Consistency with u.u = -1 requires f.u = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after Example 8.10 by putting the applied force on the right-hand side, used for polar-coordinate mechanics in Example 8.11, boxed as the chapter summary equation, and the orthogonality f.u = 0 is left to Exercise 8.4.
formulas: m\left(\frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\tau}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm d\tau}\right) = f^\mu

concepts.name: connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates
concepts.definition: In flat 2D polar coordinates (r, theta) the only non-zero connection coefficients are Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r and Gamma^theta_{r theta} = Gamma^theta_{theta r} = 1/r; in the geodesic equation they produce the centrifugal term -r thetadot^2 and the Coriolis-like term 2 rdot thetadot / r.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 7 in a margin note and used in Example 8.11 to show that uniform circular motion needs an inward force, and in Exercise 8.1 to find straight lines in polar form.
concepts.notes: The theta equation is a coordinate-basis component (units of angular acceleration); multiply by r for the physical tangential component.

concepts.name: connection coefficients
concepts.definition: The coefficients that tell how coordinate basis vectors change from point to point, entering the covariant derivative as (nabla_u v)^mu = u^alpha(partial_alpha v^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} v^beta).
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from Chapter 7; this chapter uses them and reads them off equations of motion, while computing them from the metric is deferred to Chapter 9.
formulas: (\nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u)^\mu = u^\alpha\left(\frac{\partial u^\mu}{\partial x^\alpha} + u^\beta\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\right)

concepts.name: null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic whose tangent has zero norm; light rays and other massless free particles move on them. It has no proper time, is parametrized by an affine parameter sigma with g_{mu nu} dx^mu/dsigma dx^nu/dsigma = 0, and at every point it runs along the surface of the local light cone.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in margin notes 1 and 8, then made the topic of §8.4 with Fig. 8.5 showing light cones tangent to a curved null world line.

concepts.name: spacelike geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic with spacelike tangent, found by making the proper length integral of (+ds^2)^(1/2) stationary; no physical particle travels along one (tachyons aside), but such curves are useful geometric tools.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 1, as a counterpart to timelike geodesics; the plane and sphere examples are Riemannian analogues.

concepts.name: null condition method for light rays
concepts.definition: Instead of solving the null geodesic equation, impose ds^2 = 0 on the line element along an assumed path to obtain the coordinate velocity dx/dt of light and integrate; adequate when the path shape is known or a small bending can be ignored.
concepts.how_introduced: Recommended at the start of §8.4 as the simple way to analyse light and demonstrated in Example 8.12.
concepts.notes: It fixes the speed along the path but not the path itself; the straight-line assumption in the Shapiro calculation is justified only to first order in GM.

concepts.name: weak-field metric with spatial curvature term
concepts.definition: The first-order metric outside a weak static source, ds^2 = -(1 + 2 Phi) dt^2 + (1 - 2 Phi)(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2) with Phi = -GM/r; the time part alone gives Newtonian motion of slow particles, but both parts contribute equally to the propagation of light.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in Example 8.12 as the more accurate version of eqn 8.30, with derivation deferred to §14.1 and Chapter 45.
prerequisites: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation
concepts.notes: Without the spatial factor the Shapiro delay would come out half as large; the book does not point this out.

concepts.name: coordinate speed of light
aliases: dx/dt of light in a gravitational field
concepts.definition: The rate at which a light signal's coordinate position changes with coordinate time; in the weak field it is (1 + 2 Phi)^(1/2)(1 - 2 Phi)^(-1/2) ≈ 1 - 2GM/r, slower near a mass, even though every local observer measures c.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in Example 8.12 from ds^2 = 0; the book links it back to the Chapter 5 light-cone discussion.
prerequisites: null condition method for light rays
weak-field metric with spatial curvature term
concepts.notes: Printed eqn 8.38 has the ratio inverted and GM where 2GM is needed; see gaps_and_pitfalls.

concepts.name: Shapiro time delay
concepts.definition: The extra coordinate travel time of a light or radar signal passing a mass, which for a path with closest approach b between distances d_p and d_e is 2GM ln(4 d_p d_e / b^2) (divide by c^3 in SI), arising because light's coordinate speed is reduced near the mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 8.12: integrate dt = (1 + 2GM/r) dx along a straight line with closest approach b, leg by leg, using the standard integral of 1/sqrt(x^2 + a^2).
prerequisites: null condition method for light rays

concepts.name: classical solar-system tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: The historic tests perihelion precession of Mercury, deflection of starlight by the Sun, and gravitational redshift, joined later by the radar time-delay test proposed by Irwin Shapiro.
concepts.how_introduced: Unnumbered margin note beside the Shapiro delay, pointing forward to Chapters 23 and 13.

concepts.name: proper time
concepts.definition: Time measured by a clock carried along a timelike world line, d tau = (-ds^2)^(1/2); it is the natural affine parameter for massive free particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from earlier chapters; here it is the functional extremized by timelike geodesics and the physical meaning of length parametrization.

concepts.name: line element
concepts.definition: The squared infinitesimal interval ds^2 = g_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu between neighbouring points, whose integrated square root gives lengths or proper times along curves.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the start of the geometric part of §8.1 as the input from which the length functional is built.

concepts.name: parallel transport
aliases: transporting a vector without turning it
concepts.definition: Moving a vector v along a curve with tangent u so that its covariant derivative vanishes, nabla_u v = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 7 in §8.2 to give the self-parallel definition of a geodesic.

concepts.name: covariant derivative along a curve
concepts.definition: The derivative of a vector field along a curve corrected by connection terms so that the result is a vector: (nabla_u v)^mu = u^alpha(partial_alpha v^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} v^beta) = dv^mu/dlambda + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^alpha v^beta.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from Chapter 7 for the component expansion in §8.2; Exercise 8.4 adds the version for 1-forms with the opposite-sign connection term.

concepts.name: light cone
concepts.definition: The set of null directions at a point, bounding the directions available to massive particles; a null geodesic is everywhere tangent to it.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 8.5 draws small cones along a curved null world line; Example 8.12 refers back to Chapter 5 for light-cone structure from the null condition.

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Results showing that, under energy conditions, families of geodesics must focus (develop conjugate points), which implies geodesic incompleteness such as a Big-Bang singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Only a forward pointer in margin note 2, as the important application of conjugate points.

concepts.name: tachyon
concepts.definition: A speculative particle that would move faster than light and hence along spacelike world lines; no such particle is known.
concepts.how_introduced: Parenthetical aside in margin note 1 on spacelike geodesics.

concepts.name: geodesic equation from a freely falling frame
aliases: equivalence-principle derivation of the geodesic equation
concepts.definition: Starting from xi^mu with d^2 xi^mu/dtau^2 = 0 in the particle's comoving freely falling coordinates and transforming to arbitrary coordinates x^nu by the chain rule, the second-derivative terms of the transformation assemble into a connection term, reproducing the geodesic equation without any prior geometry.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 8.3 frames it as what one would be forced to write even without knowing about curvature.
formulas: \frac{\mathrm d^2x^\nu}{\mathrm d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial\xi^\mu}\frac{\partial^2\xi^\mu}{\partial x^\lambda\partial x^\sigma}\frac{\mathrm dx^\lambda}{\mathrm d\tau}\frac{\mathrm dx^\sigma}{\mathrm d\tau} = 0

key_equations.name: Free-particle action
key_equations.meaning: Action of a free massive particle is minus its mass times proper time, so its stationary paths are stationary-proper-time curves, i.e. timelike geodesics.
key_equations.symbols: m mass; ds^2 line element; tau proper time; c = 1

key_equations.name: Proper length for spacelike curves
key_equations.meaning: Functional whose stationary curves are spacelike geodesics.

key_equations.name: Free motion in flat spacetime
key_equations.meaning: With no forces and no curvature, 4-coordinates in inertial coordinates have zero second derivative with respect to proper time.
key_equations.symbols: x^mu inertial coordinates; tau proper time

key_equations.name: Straight world lines
key_equations.meaning: General solution of (8.1): straight world lines, the geodesics of Minkowski spacetime.

key_equations.name: Linear response of a swarm of trajectories
key_equations.meaning: Small changes of initial momenta map linearly to changes of final position; a conjugate point is where this map becomes singular (non-zero delta p gives zero delta q).
key_equations.symbols: q^i positions; p^j initial momenta; N_ij response matrix

key_equations.name: Line element and total interval
key_equations.latex: \mathrm ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu}\mathrm dx^\mu\mathrm dx^\nu, \qquad s = \int\sqrt{|\mathrm ds^2|}
key_equations.meaning: The metric builds the interval whose stationary value defines geodesics; whether it is a minimum or maximum depends on the signature.

key_equations.name: Interval as an action
key_equations.latex: s = \int\sqrt{|\mathrm ds^2|} = \int\mathrm d\lambda\left|\left(\frac{\mathrm ds}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2\right|^{1/2} = \int\mathrm d\lambda\,L(x^\mu,\dot x^\mu)
key_equations.meaning: Rewrites the interval as a parameter integral whose integrand serves as the Lagrangian for the Euler-Lagrange equations.
key_equations.symbols: lambda curve parameter; L Lagrangian; dot = d/dlambda

key_equations.name: Euclidean plane line element
key_equations.meaning: Flat 2D metric in Cartesian coordinates.

key_equations.name: Plane Lagrangian
key_equations.latex: L = \frac{\mathrm ds}{\mathrm d\lambda} = \left[\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Length Lagrangian for the plane.

key_equations.name: Plane Euler-Lagrange ingredients
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial(\mathrm dx/\mathrm d\lambda)} = \frac1L\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = 0
key_equations.meaning: First derivatives taken before any choice of parameter; the 1/L factor is what length parametrization later removes.

key_equations.name: Chain rule for velocity under reparametrization
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda} = \frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\eta}\frac{\mathrm d\eta}{\mathrm d\lambda}
key_equations.meaning: How velocities transform under lambda = lambda(eta); used to show the length is parameter independent.

key_equations.name: Measure under reparametrization
key_equations.meaning: Change of measure that cancels the factors from (8.7) inside the square root.

key_equations.name: Reparametrization invariance of length
key_equations.latex: s = \int\mathrm d\lambda\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2\right]^{1/2} = \int\mathrm d\eta\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\eta}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm d\eta}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: The length integral keeps its form in any parameter, so the parameter is a free choice.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange equation for x
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\partial L}{\partial(\mathrm dx/\mathrm d\lambda)} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}
key_equations.meaning: Margin reminder that the parameter appears on both sides and effectively cancels, which is why it may be chosen after differentiation.

key_equations.name: Length parametrization in the plane
key_equations.meaning: Choosing d lambda = ds sets the Lagrangian to one on the solution, simplifying the equations and supplying a constraint.

key_equations.name: Plane geodesic equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\left(\frac1L\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right) = \frac{\mathrm d^2x}{\mathrm d\lambda^2} = 0
key_equations.meaning: With L = 1 the Euler-Lagrange equation reduces to zero second derivative; likewise for y.

key_equations.name: Straight line
key_equations.meaning: Candidate solution checked against (8.11).

key_equations.name: Straight-line velocities
key_equations.meaning: With x = lambda the velocities are constant, so second derivatives vanish. Note that this trial parametrization gives L = (1 + m^2)^(1/2) rather than 1, so it is not arc length; the check still works because the equations only need constant velocities.

key_equations.name: Unit-sphere metric
key_equations.meaning: Line element on a sphere of radius 1.

key_equations.name: Sphere length functional
key_equations.latex: s = \int\mathrm d\lambda\left[\left(\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2 + \sin^2\theta\left(\frac{\mathrm d\phi}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Parametrized interval on the sphere, the action for geodesics.

key_equations.name: Sphere Euler-Lagrange ingredients
key_equations.meaning: First-stage partial derivatives before setting L = 1; the vanishing phi derivative signals a conserved quantity.
key_equations.symbols: Dots are d/dlambda. The derivatives in the first row are with respect to thetadot and phidot; the overdots on the denominators are easy to miss in print and are lost in the text export.

key_equations.name: Sphere: lambda-derivatives with L = 1
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta} = \ddot\theta, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\phi} = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\theta\dot\phi + \sin^2\theta\,\ddot\phi
key_equations.meaning: Left-hand sides of the Euler-Lagrange equations after length parametrization.
key_equations.symbols: The book prints the second right-hand side as 2 sin theta thetadot phidot + sin^2 theta phiddot, omitting cos theta; the correct derivative of sin^2 theta phidot contains 2 sin theta cos theta thetadot phidot, as confirmed by (8.18).

key_equations.name: Expanded phi equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d^2\phi}{\mathrm d\lambda^2} + 2\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\mathrm d\phi}{\mathrm d\lambda} = 0
key_equations.meaning: Expanded form of (8.20); its coefficient 2 cot theta is twice the connection coefficient Gamma^phi_{theta phi} of the sphere.

key_equations.name: Sphere geodesic equation (theta)
key_equations.meaning: Motion in phi pushes the curve away from a latitude circle unless theta = pi/2; latitude circles other than the equator are not geodesics.

key_equations.name: Sphere geodesic equation (phi)
key_equations.meaning: Conservation of angular momentum about the polar axis along a geodesic.

key_equations.name: Covariant acceleration
key_equations.latex: \mathbf a = \frac{\mathrm D\mathbf u}{\mathrm d\tau} = \nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u
key_equations.meaning: The coordinate-independent 4-acceleration; zero for free fall.

key_equations.name: Geometric geodesic equation
key_equations.meaning: A geodesic parallel transports its own tangent vector; valid for any causal type and affine parameter.
key_equations.symbols: u tangent vector; lambda affine parameter

key_equations.name: Components of nabla_u u
key_equations.latex: (\nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u)^\mu = u^\alpha\left(\frac{\partial u^\mu}{\partial x^\alpha} + u^\beta\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\right) = 0
key_equations.meaning: Component expansion using the Chapter 7 covariant derivative.

key_equations.name: Substituting u = dx/dlambda
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\partial u^\mu}{\partial x^\alpha} + \frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm d\lambda}\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta} = 0
key_equations.meaning: The first term is the chain-rule derivative of u^mu along the curve.

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm d\lambda^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\lambda}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm d\lambda} = 0
key_equations.meaning: Ordinary acceleration plus a connection term vanishes along a geodesic; with lambda = tau it is the force-free equation of motion in curved spacetime.
key_equations.symbols: x^mu coordinates; Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} connection coefficients; lambda affine parameter

key_equations.name: Affine reparametrization
key_equations.meaning: The allowed relabelings of proper time that preserve the form of the geodesic equation.

key_equations.name: Null condition with an affine parameter
key_equations.meaning: Photon world lines have zero interval, so they are parametrized by an affine parameter sigma rather than proper time.
key_equations.symbols: sigma affine parameter. The margin text afterwards refers to dx^sigma where dx^mu is meant.

key_equations.name: Conservation of the tangent norm
key_equations.latex: \nabla_{\mathbf u}(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) = 2\,\mathbf u\cdot(\nabla_{\mathbf u}\mathbf u) = 0
key_equations.meaning: u.u is constant along a geodesic, so its timelike, null or spacelike character never changes.

key_equations.name: Geometric momentum conservation
key_equations.meaning: Free-particle 4-momentum is parallel transported along itself; for photons this is the null geodesic equation.

key_equations.name: Components of nabla_p p
key_equations.latex: (\nabla_{\mathbf p}\mathbf p)^\beta = m u^\alpha\left(p^\beta{}_{,\alpha} + \Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\sigma}p^\sigma\right) = m\left(\frac{\mathrm dp^\beta}{\mathrm d\tau} + u^\alpha p^\sigma\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\sigma}\right)
key_equations.meaning: Shows nabla_p p reduces to m dp/dtau where the connection vanishes (a LIF).

key_equations.name: Inertial force
key_equations.meaning: The connection term of the geodesic equation viewed as a force; it may come from coordinates or from curvature.
key_equations.symbols: dot = d/dtau; lambda here is a dummy index, not the parameter

key_equations.name: Swingball force balance (players' frame)
key_equations.meaning: Vertical tension balances weight; horizontal tension supplies the centripetal force. In the ball's frame an outward centrifugal F balances T sin theta.
key_equations.symbols: T tension; theta string angle from the pole; v speed; r orbit radius

key_equations.name: Weak-field metric (time part only)
key_equations.meaning: Minimal metric that reproduces Newtonian gravity for slow particles.
key_equations.symbols: Phi Newtonian potential; G = c = 1 units with GM a length

key_equations.name: Weak-field equation of motion
key_equations.meaning: Spatial geodesic equations for metric (8.30); reduces to Newton's law when tau ≈ t.

key_equations.name: Gravitational connection coefficients
key_equations.meaning: The connection coefficient carries the Newtonian gravitational field; -Gamma^i_tt is the gravitational acceleration.

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation with external force
key_equations.latex: m\left(\frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm d\tau^2} + \frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\tau}\frac{\mathrm dx^\lambda}{\mathrm d\tau}\Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\lambda}\right) = f^\mu
key_equations.meaning: An applied 4-force produces a covariant acceleration; zero force gives geodesic motion.

key_equations.name: Non-relativistic forced geodesic equation
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm dt^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm dt}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{f^\mu}{m}
key_equations.meaning: Version with tau ≈ t used for Newtonian mechanics in curvilinear coordinates.

key_equations.name: Radial equation in polar coordinates
key_equations.latex: \frac{f^r}{m} = \frac{\mathrm d^2r}{\mathrm dt^2} + \Gamma^r_{\alpha\beta}u^\alpha u^\beta = a^r + \Gamma^r_{\theta\theta}u^\theta u^\theta = a^r - r(u^\theta)^2
key_equations.meaning: Radial applied force equals radial coordinate acceleration minus the centrifugal term; uniform circular motion (a^r = 0) needs an inward force m r thetadot^2.

key_equations.name: Angular equation in polar coordinates
key_equations.latex: \frac{f^\theta}{m} = \frac{\mathrm d^2\theta}{\mathrm dt^2} + \Gamma^\theta_{\alpha\beta}u^\alpha u^\beta = a^\theta + 2\Gamma^\theta_{r\theta}u^r u^\theta = a^\theta + \frac{2u^r u^\theta}{r}
key_equations.meaning: The Coriolis-like term 2 rdot thetadot / r appears from the connection; with u^r = 0 no tangential force is needed for uniform rotation.
key_equations.symbols: factor 2 from the symmetric pair Gamma^theta_{r theta} = Gamma^theta_{theta r}

key_equations.name: Weak-field metric with spatial correction
key_equations.meaning: More accurate weak-field metric needed for light, whose motion is affected by the spatial part as much as by the time part.

key_equations.name: Coordinate speed of light (as printed)
key_equations.meaning: Intended as the coordinate velocity of light from ds^2 = 0. As printed it is inconsistent with (8.37) and (8.39): imposing ds^2 = 0 on (8.37) along a line gives dr/dt = [(1 + 2 Phi)/(1 - 2 Phi)]^(1/2) = [(r - 2GM)/(r + 2GM)]^(1/2), i.e. dt/dr = [(r + 2GM)/(r - 2GM)]^(1/2) ≈ 1 + 2GM/r, which is what (8.39) uses.

key_equations.name: Coordinate travel time
key_equations.meaning: First-order travel time along a straight coordinate path; the 2GM/r part is the delay integrand.

key_equations.name: Standard integral
key_equations.meaning: Integral used to evaluate the delay along each leg.

key_equations.name: One-leg delay
key_equations.meaning: For a leg from closest approach to distance x0 with b << x0, the delay grows logarithmically with distance.

key_equations.name: Shapiro time delay
key_equations.meaning: Total one-way excess coordinate time for a signal from planet to Earth grazing the Sun; in SI multiply GM by 1/c^3. Radar echo experiments measure twice this.
key_equations.symbols: d_p, d_e distances of planet and Earth from the point of closest approach; b impact parameter

key_equations.name: Master equation of motion (summary)
key_equations.latex: m\left(\frac{\mathrm d^2x^\mu}{\mathrm d\tau^2} + \Gamma^\mu_{\alpha\beta}\frac{\mathrm dx^\alpha}{\mathrm d\tau}\frac{\mathrm dx^\beta}{\mathrm d\tau}\right) = f^\mu
key_equations.meaning: Relates acceleration to geometry (connection, giving inertial forces) and to external forces; f = 0 is the geodesic equation.

key_equations.name: Flat length in polar coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Starting functional for Exercise 8.1.

key_equations.name: Polar geodesic equations
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d^2r}{\mathrm d\lambda^2} = r\left(\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right)^2, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\lambda}\left(r^2\frac{\mathrm d\theta}{\mathrm d\lambda}\right) = 0
key_equations.meaning: Geodesics of the plane in polar coordinates: centrifugal-like radial equation and conserved angular momentum.

key_equations.name: Radial profile of a line
key_equations.meaning: With lambda arc length from closest approach, distance from the origin grows hyperbolically.

key_equations.name: Angular rate along a line
key_equations.meaning: From r^2 thetadot = a.

key_equations.name: Parametric polar line
key_equations.meaning: Integrated angular equation.

key_equations.name: Polar equation of a straight line
key_equations.meaning: Straight line in polar form, interpreted with Fig. 8.7.

key_equations.name: Cartesian-to-polar line parameters
key_equations.meaning: Substitutions linking alpha x + beta y = gamma to (8.48) in Exercise 8.2(b).

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation from a comoving frame
key_equations.latex: \frac{\mathrm d^2x^\nu}{\mathrm d\tau^2} + \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial\xi^\mu}\frac{\partial^2\xi^\mu}{\partial x^\lambda\partial x^\sigma}\frac{\mathrm dx^\lambda}{\mathrm d\tau}\frac{\mathrm dx^\sigma}{\mathrm d\tau} = 0
key_equations.meaning: Transforming xi-ddot = 0 from the particle's freely falling frame yields the geodesic equation with Gamma^nu_{lambda sigma} = (partial x^nu / partial xi^mu)(partial^2 xi^mu / partial x^lambda partial x^sigma).

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a 1-form
key_equations.meaning: Expansion in basis 1-forms, previewing Part V.

key_equations.name: 1-form covariant derivative components
key_equations.meaning: Lower-index version with a minus-sign connection term.

figures.label: Fig. 8.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two points on a sphere joined by both arcs of one great circle; the antipode of the starting point is marked as its conjugate point.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing of a sphere as a circle outline. A great circle is drawn as a tilted ellipse. An open circle labelled q1 sits near the bottom, a filled dot q2 on the left front, and a filled dot q1* at the upper right near the rim. The front half of the great circle is solid: a short arc runs from q1 up to q2 with an arrowhead pointing up, and a longer arc comes down from q1* to q2 with an arrowhead pointing toward q2. The back half is dashed and carries an arrowhead running from q1 up and to the right toward q1*. Short dash-dot fragments near the lower rim suggest the hidden side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Between two non-antipodal points there are two geodesics on the same great circle: the short direct one (i) and the long one (ii) that passes through the antipode q1*, which is a saddle of the action rather than a minimum.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere

redesign.idea: Globe with two draggable points and both great-circle routes, each tagged with its length and with a live 'minimum or saddle' verdict.
redesign.interaction: Drag q1 and q2 on a rotatable 3D sphere; toggle between route (i) and route (ii); a wiggle slider perturbs the chosen route sideways and a small plot shows length versus wiggle amplitude for sideways and along-path perturbations, rising in all directions for (i) and dropping in one direction for (ii) once it passes the antipode.

figures.label: Fig. 8.1(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A spray of free particles launched from one point on a sphere spreads out and then reconverges at the antipodal conjugate point.
figures.visual_description: Sphere outline with a web of curves resembling meridians. Near the lower left a point labelled q1 (with a curved pointer) has many short arrows radiating outward in a starburst, some drawn dotted as if on the far side. The curves fan out from q1 across the sphere and all converge at a single point near the top right, labelled q1* with another curved pointer, where several arrowheads crowd together.
figures.what_it_teaches: Geodesic focusing: neighbouring geodesics from one point meet again at the conjugate point, which is the physical test for whether a path through it is a minimum.

redesign.idea: Launch a fan of geodesics from any point on a sphere, plane or saddle and watch whether they refocus.
redesign.interaction: Click to set the launch point, drag to set the fan width and number of rays; press play to animate particles moving at equal speed; a readout marks the first focus and its distance (pi on a unit sphere). Switching the surface to a plane or saddle shows no refocusing, setting up geodesic deviation and Raychaudhuri focusing later.

figures.label: Fig. 8.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A timelike curve can be shadowed ever more closely by a chain of light-like segments, each of zero interval.
figures.visual_description: Small hand-drawn sketch of a smooth, gently wavy curve running roughly vertically, with 'TIMELIKE CURVE' hand-lettered along its middle. About eight small open circles sit on or beside the curve, and short straight segments join successive circles into a chain that winds back and forth across the curve, hugging it closely from bottom to top. The drawing is schematic: the segments are not shown at 45 degrees and no axes or light cones are drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: Proper time along timelike paths has no positive lower bound, since paths made of null pieces have zero total interval yet lie arbitrarily close to any timelike curve; timelike geodesics therefore maximize rather than minimize proper time.
concepts: null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve
maximal proper time of timelike geodesics

redesign.idea: Spacetime diagram where the learner replaces a timelike world line by a zigzag of near-light-speed segments and watches the clock reading collapse.
redesign.interaction: Slider for the number of zigzag segments N and a second for how close each segment's speed is to c; the page draws the zigzag at 45 degrees around the smooth world line and shows proper times of the straight geodesic, the smooth curve and the zigzag, with the zigzag's value tending to zero while its shape converges to the curve.

figures.label: Fig. 8.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Three curves on a sphere: a meridian from the pole and the equator are geodesics, a circle of latitude is not.
figures.visual_description: Sphere outline with a hand-lettered 'north pole' label and a short dashed tick above a dot at the top. A solid curve A runs down the front from the pole to the equator, meeting it with a small right-angle mark. The equator B is a solid arc across the front. A dashed ellipse C near the top is a circle of latitude. Some hatching marks the lower left edge of the equator region.
figures.what_it_teaches: The derived equations select meridians and the equator (great circles) and reject latitude circles, making concrete that 'constant coordinate' is not the same as 'straight'.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere

redesign.idea: Geodesic tester on a globe: draw or pick a curve and see the residuals of the two geodesic equations along it, plus a car-steering view.
redesign.interaction: Choose a latitude slider for a circle of constant theta or tilt a great circle; the page evaluates thetaddot - sin theta cos theta phidot^2 along the curve and colours it green when zero; a first-person 'drive along the curve' view shows the steering-wheel angle needed, zero only for great circles.

figures.label: Fig. 8.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Swingball seen from the players (tension supplies the centripetal force) and from the ball (a centrifugal force appears).
figures.visual_description: Panel (a): a vertical pole with a string running from its top down and to the right to a filled ball; the angle theta is marked between pole and string; an arrow labelled T points along the string toward the pole; a dotted horizontal ellipse shows the ball's circular path; a horizontal arrow from the ball points inward toward the pole axis, and an arrow labelled mg points down. Panel (b): a free-body diagram of the ball as a dot with four arrows: up |T| cos theta, down mg, left |T| sin theta, and right F.
figures.what_it_teaches: The same physical situation needs an unbalanced centripetal force in one frame and a balancing outward inertial force in the other; inertial forces are frame-dependent bookkeeping that nonetheless have measurable effects in that frame.

redesign.idea: Split-screen tetherball: lab frame and co-rotating frame side by side with live free-body diagrams.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for rotation speed and string length; theta adjusts so T cos theta = mg; left panel shows the ball circling with the net inward force; right panel rotates with the ball and shows the centrifugal arrow F equal to mv^2/r; a toggle 'cut the string' shows a straight line in the lab frame and a curving path with centrifugal and Coriolis deflection in the rotating frame.

figures.label: Fig. 8.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light ray's world line is null: at every point it lies along the local light cone.
figures.visual_description: A smooth S-shaped curve rising from lower left to upper right. At about five points along it small cones with dotted inner outlines are drawn with their apex on the curve, tilted so that the curve runs along one edge of each cone; the cone at the top right is drawn larger. The cones point in different directions following the bending of the curve.
figures.what_it_teaches: A null geodesic in curved spacetime need not look straight in coordinates, but locally it always moves at light speed, tangent to the light cone.

redesign.idea: Light-cone field on a 2D spacetime diagram of a weak or strong gravitational field, with a light ray traced through it.
redesign.interaction: Drag a mass parameter to tilt and narrow the local cones (coordinate speed of light 1 - 2GM/r); click to launch a light ray that is integrated so its tangent always sits on a cone edge; compare with a massive particle launched from the same event staying inside the cones.

figures.label: Fig. 8.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Geometry of the time-delay calculation: a signal travels from a planet past the Sun to Earth.
figures.visual_description: A vertical straight line with a filled dot labelled e at the top and an open dot labelled p at the bottom. To its left, a circle labelled S represents the Sun, joined to the line by a horizontal double-headed arrow labelled b. Distances d_e (from the foot of b up to e) and d_p (from the foot down to p) are marked with arrows meeting at the foot point. A separate upward arrow on the right labelled x shows the direction of the coordinate axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: The delay integral is set up along a straight coordinate line with impact parameter b, split into two legs at the point of closest approach.

redesign.idea: Solar-conjunction radar simulator that turns the logarithm into microseconds.
redesign.interaction: Drag the planet around its orbit relative to Earth; b updates as the line of sight approaches the Sun's limb; a plot of round-trip delay versus days from conjunction shows the sharp logarithmic spike (about 250 microseconds for Mars when grazing the limb); toggles to drop the spatial metric term (halving the delay) and to switch planets.

figures.label: Fig. 8.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Polar description of a straight line: its perpendicular distance from the origin and the direction of that perpendicular.
figures.visual_description: An origin at lower left with a horizontal reference ray to the right. A straight line slants up to the right above the origin. A segment labelled a drops from the origin perpendicular to the line, with a right-angle box at its foot. A second segment labelled r runs from the origin to a general point on the line. Arcs at the origin mark theta0 (from the reference ray to the perpendicular) and theta (from the reference ray to r).
figures.what_it_teaches: The complicated-looking polar solution r = a / cos(theta - theta0) is simply a straight line: right-triangle trigonometry with a and theta0 as the line's parameters.
concepts: straight lines as geodesics of flat space
connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates

redesign.idea: Straight line in polar dress: the same geodesic displayed as a Cartesian line and as polar equations solved step by step.
redesign.interaction: Drag the line; a and theta0 update; a point slides along the line with arc length lambda from the foot while side plots show r(lambda) = sqrt(lambda^2 + a^2) and theta(lambda), and a vector readout shows r thetadot^2 (the centrifugal term) being exactly what keeps rddot non-zero for a straight line.

worked_examples.label: Example 8.1
worked_examples.problem: Find the force-free paths in Minkowski spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Replace the Newtonian zero-acceleration law by zero second derivative of each coordinate with respect to proper time, then integrate twice.
worked_examples.key_insight: In flat spacetime and inertial coordinates the geodesic equation has no connection term, so geodesics are straight world lines; this is the baseline that curvature or curvilinear coordinates modify.
concepts: straight lines as geodesics of flat space

worked_examples.label: Example 8.2
worked_examples.problem: For free motion on a sphere between two non-antipodal points, decide which of the two great-circle routes is a minimum of the action.
worked_examples.method: Compare the direct arc (i) with the long arc (ii) through the antipode. Launch a family of particles from q1 with slightly different momenta, describe the final spread by a linear map delta q = N delta p, and observe that on the sphere they all reconverge at the antipode q1*.
worked_examples.key_insight: A trajectory that passes through a conjugate point (where nearby trajectories refocus, making N singular) is a saddle of the action, not a minimum; stationary does not mean least.
worked_examples.result: Route (i) minimizes the action; route (ii) is a saddle point.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere

worked_examples.label: Example 8.3
worked_examples.problem: Determine whether geodesics minimize or maximize the interval for Riemannian versus Lorentzian metrics.
worked_examples.method: For positive-definite metrics note that lengths are bounded below but not above. For Lorentzian metrics construct timelike curves that approximate a given one by chains of null segments (Fig. 8.2), whose interval is zero.
worked_examples.key_insight: Signature flips the character of the extremum: shortest paths in space, longest proper time in spacetime (if an extremum exists), and even a Riemannian geodesic need not be globally shortest.
worked_examples.result: Riemannian geodesics are locally length-minimizing; timelike geodesics are curves of maximal proper time.
concepts: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve

worked_examples.problem: Show that the length of a curve does not depend on how it is parametrized.
worked_examples.method: Write lambda = lambda(eta), transform each velocity with the chain rule and the measure d lambda with its Jacobian, and simplify inside the square root (margin note 3).
worked_examples.key_insight: The Jacobian factors cancel exactly because L is homogeneous of degree one in the velocities, leaving the parameter as a free gauge choice.
worked_examples.result: s = integral d eta [(dx/d eta)^2 + (dy/d eta)^2]^(1/2), same form as before.
concepts: reparametrization invariance of the length functional

worked_examples.label: Example 8.4
worked_examples.problem: Set up the Euler-Lagrange equations for the shortest path between two points in the Euclidean plane.
worked_examples.method: Write L = [(dx/dlambda)^2 + (dy/dlambda)^2]^(1/2) and compute partial L / partial xdot = xdot / L and partial L / partial x = 0, similarly for y.
worked_examples.key_insight: Even the simplest geodesic problem produces a 1/L factor that makes the equations awkward until a parametrization is chosen.
concepts: Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional

worked_examples.label: Example 8.5
worked_examples.problem: Complete the plane calculation using length parametrization.
worked_examples.method: Set L = 1 after differentiation so that the Euler-Lagrange equations reduce to second derivatives of x and y vanishing; verify with x = lambda, y = m lambda + c.
worked_examples.key_insight: Length parametrization turns geodesic equations into 'acceleration = 0' in Cartesian coordinates, making contact with Newton's first law.
concepts: straight lines as geodesics of flat space

worked_examples.label: Example 8.6
worked_examples.problem: Find the geodesic equations on the unit sphere and identify simple solutions.
worked_examples.method: Build L from ds^2 = d theta^2 + sin^2 theta d phi^2, take partial derivatives with respect to theta, phi and their rates, set L = 1, and assemble the two Euler-Lagrange equations; test meridians, the equator and a latitude circle (margin note 7, Fig. 8.3).
worked_examples.key_insight: The theta equation contains a sin theta cos theta phidot^2 term that vanishes only on the equator, so latitude circles fail; the phi equation is a conservation law because phi does not appear in L.
worked_examples.result: thetaddot - sin theta cos theta phidot^2 = 0 and d/dlambda(sin^2 theta phidot) = 0; solved by theta = lambda, phi = 0 and by theta = pi/2, phi = lambda, not by theta = pi/4, phi = lambda.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere
Euler-Lagrange equations for the length functional

worked_examples.problem: Derive the component geodesic equation from the geometric condition that a free particle has zero covariant acceleration.
worked_examples.method: Write a = nabla_u u = 0, expand with the covariant derivative u^alpha(partial_alpha u^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} u^beta), substitute u^alpha = dx^alpha/dlambda and recognize the first term as d^2x^mu/dlambda^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: The geodesic equation is just 'ordinary acceleration plus a connection correction equals zero', the curved-coordinates version of xddot = 0.

worked_examples.label: Example 8.7
worked_examples.problem: Show that a geodesic cannot change from timelike to null or spacelike.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate u.u along the geodesic with the Leibniz rule and use nabla_u u = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Norm conservation is automatic for geodesics, which is why u.u = -1 can be imposed once as a constraint.
concepts: conservation of u.u along a geodesic

worked_examples.label: Example 8.8
worked_examples.problem: Justify the geometric momentum conservation law nabla_p p = 0.
worked_examples.method: Expand (nabla_p p)^beta = m(dp^beta/dtau + u^alpha p^sigma Gamma^beta_{alpha sigma}); pass to a local inertial frame where Gamma vanishes so it becomes flat-space dp/dtau = 0; invoke general covariance to extend the tensor equation to all frames; note in a margin that photon momentum is tangent to its null world line.
worked_examples.key_insight: A standard two-step GR proof pattern: verify a tensor law where the connection vanishes, then promote it covariantly.
worked_examples.result: nabla_p p = 0 in every frame, for massive particles and photons.

worked_examples.label: Example 8.9
worked_examples.problem: Analyse swingball (tetherball) forces in the players' frame and in the ball's frame.
worked_examples.method: In the lab: resolve tension into vertical T cos theta = mg and horizontal T sin theta = mv^2/r as centripetal force. In the ball's frame: no horizontal acceleration, so an outward centrifugal force F must balance T sin theta.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inertial forces are what a non-inertial frame must add to make Newton's law hold; they are the everyday model for how connection terms act like forces.
worked_examples.result: F = T sin theta = mv^2/r, directed outward in the ball's frame.

worked_examples.label: Example 8.10
worked_examples.problem: Recover Newtonian gravity from the geodesic equation for a weak static field.
worked_examples.method: Take ds^2 = -(1 + 2 Phi) dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2, quote the resulting spatial equation of motion (method in Chapter 9), and identify Gamma^i_tt by comparison with the geodesic equation; use tau ≈ t for slow motion.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gravity appears through a single connection component built from the gradient of g_tt; the 'force' is an inertial force in the sense of §8.3.
worked_examples.result: Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi = GM x^i / r^3, giving xddot^i = -GM x^i / r^3.
concepts: Newtonian limit of the geodesic equation

worked_examples.label: Example 8.11
worked_examples.problem: Write Newton's second law in plane polar coordinates using the forced geodesic equation.
worked_examples.method: Insert the polar connection coefficients Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r and Gamma^theta_{r theta} = 1/r into (8.34) with tau ≈ t and separate radial and angular components.
worked_examples.key_insight: The familiar centrifugal (-r thetadot^2) and Coriolis-like (2 rdot thetadot / r) terms are nothing but connection coefficients, so uniform circular motion is not a geodesic and needs a centripetal force.
worked_examples.result: f^r/m = rddot - r thetadot^2; f^theta/m = thetaddot + 2 rdot thetadot / r.
concepts: connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates

worked_examples.label: Example 8.12
worked_examples.problem: Compute the extra travel time of a light signal from a planet to Earth passing close to the Sun.
worked_examples.method: Impose ds^2 = 0 on the weak-field metric with both time and space perturbations; expand to first order in GM/r to get dt = (1 + 2GM/r) dx along a straight line at impact parameter b; integrate each leg using the integral of 1/sqrt(x^2 + b^2) and take b much smaller than the distances; add the legs.
worked_examples.key_insight: Light's coordinate speed is reduced near a mass, and the resulting delay depends only logarithmically on the geometry, giving a clean observable test.
worked_examples.result: Delta t = 2GM ln(4 d_p d_e / b^2) (times 1/c^3 in SI), about 120 microseconds one-way for a signal grazing the Sun from Mars (own estimate).
concepts: null condition method for light rays
weak-field metric with spatial curvature term

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Geodesic as the straightest line a local observer could draw
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The opening and the end of §8.2 describe geodesics as straightest possible paths, which a freely falling observer would perceive as straight lines in their locally flat neighbourhood.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: 'Straight' is local; globally geodesics can reconverge (sphere) and need not be shortest or longest.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ant-on-a-surface view: the learner walks forward without turning on a sphere and sees the resulting track drawn from outside as a great circle.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Travelling on the Earth's surface along great circles
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Two routes along one great circle, and a fan of trajectories refocusing at the antipode, make the abstract second-variation question visible.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The sphere has uniform positive curvature so all geodesics refocus at one point; in spacetime focusing depends on matter content and need not be so tidy.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flight-route globe showing the short and long great-circle routes between two cities and how neighbouring routes from one city all meet at its antipode.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Staircase of light-speed dashes shadowing a smooth path
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 8.2 shows a zigzag of null segments hugging a timelike curve, proving that proper time can be made as small as desired so no minimum exists.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The zigzag has corners (infinite accelerations) and is only close in position, not in velocity; it bounds proper time but does not by itself prove the geodesic is a maximum.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Clock race: a traveller who repeatedly dashes back and forth at near light speed around a stay-at-home path, with both clocks displayed.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A familiar playground game shows that the same motion needs a centripetal force in one frame and gains an outward centrifugal force in the other, so inertial forces are frame artefacts that feel real.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The ball is not in free fall (tension acts), and its accelerometer registers tension, not centrifugal force; in GR a freely falling observer feels no gravitational force at all, so the analogy for gravity is about coordinate bookkeeping rather than sensation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between lab and co-rotating camera for a tetherball with live force arrows, then cut the string.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Mentioned at the start of Example 8.9 as the everyday case of an accelerated frame producing forces that are not 'fictional' to those experiencing them.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a passing remark; Coriolis effects are not developed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newtonian mechanics in polar coordinates as a toy model of gravity-as-connection
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 8.11 shows that flat-space polar coordinates already generate centrifugal and Coriolis-like terms through Gamma, so learners see connection 'forces' in a setting with no curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Here all Gammas can be removed globally by going to Cartesian coordinates; gravity's Gammas can be removed only at a point.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Same free particle plotted in Cartesian and polar coordinates with the polar 'forces' r thetadot^2 and 2 rdot thetadot / r drawn as arrows that appear from nowhere.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Light cones as little funnels the ray must skim
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 8.5 draws cones tangent to a curving null world line to show that light always moves along the cone surface locally.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The cones in the drawing are schematic; in a real spacetime diagram their tilt and opening encode the metric, which the figure does not quantify.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Light-cone field that tilts with a mass slider and a ray tracer that keeps the ray on the cone edges.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A geodesic is always the shortest path, and the principle of least action always picks a minimum.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only stationarity is required. On a sphere the long great-circle route through the antipode is a geodesic but a saddle of the action, and in spacetime timelike geodesics maximize proper time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The phrases 'least action' and 'shortest distance' are how geodesics and Hamilton's principle are usually first taught.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In spacetime, the free-fall world line takes the least proper time between two events.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It takes the most: any wiggle toward null directions reduces proper time, down to zero for a chain of null segments.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Carrying over 'straight line = shortest' from Euclidean intuition; the sign flip from the minus in the metric is counterintuitive.
concepts: maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If a curve is a geodesic between two points, it must be the shortest route between them.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is only locally extremal; beyond a conjugate point, or when several geodesics join the points, a given geodesic can be longer than another.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Plane geometry has a unique geodesic between two points.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every particle in a gravitational field moves along a geodesic.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only free particles do; a charged particle in an electromagnetic field or a rocket under thrust has extra terms in its Lagrangian or a force on the right-hand side of the geodesic equation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Gravity is described as geometry, so one may assume geometry dictates all motion.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Setting L = 1 before varying is legitimate, so the Euler-Lagrange equations become trivial.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The parameter must be fixed only after the partial derivatives of L have been taken; setting L = 1 first would make everything vanish. Afterwards L = 1 is a constraint and first integral.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Length parametrization looks like a simple substitution that could be made at any stage.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A circle of constant latitude is a straight path on the sphere because one coordinate stays fixed.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the equator among latitude circles is a geodesic; elsewhere the theta equation requires sin theta cos theta phidot^2 = 0, which fails.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Constant-coordinate curves are straight lines in Cartesian coordinates, so learners equate 'coordinate line' with 'straight'.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Non-zero connection coefficients mean spacetime is curved.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Connection coefficients can be non-zero in flat space in curvilinear or accelerated coordinates (polar coordinates in Example 8.11); only curvature (Riemann tensor, Chapter 11) is coordinate-independent evidence.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Gravity is introduced through Gammas, so any Gamma looks like gravity.
concepts: connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Fictitious forces are not real, so they cannot be felt or have effects.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Within the frame that uses them they have measurable consequences and must be included for Newton's laws to balance; the book's Example 8.9 makes the point that someone riding in such a frame experiences nothing illusory about them.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The label 'fictitious' suggests they are illusions.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Uniform circular motion in flat spacetime is force-free 'coasting' because the speed is constant.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is not a geodesic: in polar coordinates a^r = 0 requires an inward applied force balancing the r thetadot^2 term.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Constant speed is confused with constant velocity.
concepts: connection coefficients in plane polar coordinates

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Photons can be tracked by their proper time like massive particles.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The interval along a null world line is zero, so proper time is unavailable; an affine parameter must be used instead.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The same geodesic equation is written with tau for massive particles.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The geodesic equation is only valid with proper time as the parameter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Any affine parameter lambda = a tau + b works; non-affine parameters add a term proportional to the tangent.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Spacelike geodesics are physically meaningless because nothing travels along them.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are useful geometric tools (for instance spatial distances and constructions), even though no known particle moves on them.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Physical relevance is equated with being a particle trajectory.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Shapiro delay means light actually slows below c near the Sun.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the coordinate speed decreases; any local observer along the path measures c. The delay is a statement about coordinate time and the extra effective path, and is observable as a comparison of round-trip times with and without the Sun near the line of sight.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian gravity comes entirely from g_tt, so the spatial part of the metric is irrelevant for light too.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: For slow particles only g_tt matters, but light is equally affected by g_ij; dropping the (1 - 2 Phi) factor would halve the Shapiro delay (and light bending).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Example 8.10 successfully uses a metric with flat spatial part.
concepts: weak-field metric with spatial curvature term

thought_experiments.name: Swarm of particles launched from one point on a sphere
thought_experiments.setup: Free particles leave q1 on a sphere with almost the same direction and speed, spreading out along neighbouring great circles.
thought_experiments.lesson: They all meet again at the antipode, the conjugate point; a path that passes such a point is a saddle rather than a minimum of the action.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated fan of geodesics on a sphere with a marker that lights up at the first focus.

thought_experiments.name: Two travellers on one great circle
thought_experiments.setup: Particles leave q1 with equal momentum in opposite directions along a great circle, one reaching q2 directly and one going the long way past the antipode.
thought_experiments.lesson: Both follow geodesics, but only the short one minimizes; the other is a saddle.
concepts: great circles as geodesics of the sphere
thought_experiments.app_idea: Race two dots in opposite directions around a great circle, with a length-versus-perturbation plot for each.

thought_experiments.name: Null zigzag traveller
thought_experiments.setup: Replace a smooth timelike trip between two events by a sequence of near-light-speed dashes that stay close to it.
thought_experiments.lesson: The zigzag traveller's clock reads almost zero, so proper time has no minimum and a timelike geodesic must be a maximum.
concepts: null zigzag approximation of a timelike curve
maximal proper time of timelike geodesics
thought_experiments.app_idea: Spacetime-diagram slider that increases the number of dashes and shows the proper-time readout collapsing.

thought_experiments.name: Swingball from the ball's point of view
thought_experiments.setup: Ride with a tethered ball circling a pole and ask what forces balance in that frame.
thought_experiments.lesson: An outward centrifugal force appears that is absent in the players' frame; inertial forces depend on the frame, as does gravity per the equivalence principle.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Co-rotating camera toggle with force arrows.

thought_experiments.name: Radar signal grazing the Sun
thought_experiments.setup: Send a light pulse from a distant planet to Earth along a line passing the Sun at closest distance b.
thought_experiments.lesson: The signal arrives later than flat-space timing predicts by an amount logarithmic in d_p d_e / b^2, a measurable fourth test of GR.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Planet-Earth-Sun configuration slider with a delay-versus-date plot.

thought_experiments.name: The particle that cannot feel its own weight
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 8.3: describe a particle in coordinates falling with it, where it has no acceleration, then re-express its motion in other coordinates.
thought_experiments.lesson: The chain rule alone forces a connection-like term into the equation of motion, so the geodesic equation follows from the equivalence principle without any knowledge of curvature.
concepts: geodesic equation from a freely falling frame

applications_and_observations.details: Signals between Earth and another planet (or spacecraft) passing close to the Sun arrive late by 2GM/c^3 ln(4 d_p d_e / b^2) each way. Radar echo measurements (round trip) double this. The book derives the formula and frames it as the fourth classical test.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 2GM_sun/c^3 ≈ 9.85 microseconds. Own estimate for a Mars signal grazing the solar limb (b ≈ 6.96e8 m, d_e ≈ 1.50e11 m, d_p ≈ 2.28e11 m): logarithm ≈ 12.5, one-way ≈ 124 microseconds, round trip ≈ 250 microseconds; for Venus ≈ 116 and 233 microseconds.

applications_and_observations.details: Gamma^i_tt = partial_i Phi reproduces the gravitational acceleration GM/r^2 for slow particles in a weak field.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: at Earth's surface Gamma^r_tt = g/c^2 ≈ 1.1e-16 per metre; for the Sun's surface GM/(c^2 R) ≈ 2.1e-6, showing the weak-field expansion parameter is tiny in the solar system.

notation_and_conventions.convention: d tau = (-ds^2)^(1/2) for timelike curves, dl = (+ds^2)^(1/2) for spacelike ones; the extremized interval is s = integral of sqrt|ds^2|.
An overdot means d/dlambda in the variational examples (margin note 5) and d/dtau in the inertial-force and polar examples (eqn 8.29, Example 8.11 with tau ≈ t).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} with the upper index first and the two symmetric lower indices contracted with velocities; (nabla_u v)^mu = u^alpha(partial_alpha v^mu + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} v^beta).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Du/dlambda and nabla_u u are used interchangeably for the derivative along a curve; comma denotes a partial derivative (p^beta_{,alpha}) and semicolon a covariant component derivative (sigma_{nu;mu}).
Bold upright letters (u, p, f) for vectors, u.v for the metric inner product; a tilde marks a 1-form and omega^nu denotes basis 1-forms.
lambda (or sigma for photons) denotes an affine parameter, related to proper time by lambda = a tau + b for massive particles.
Abbreviated LIF: coordinates where the Gammas vanish at a point.
theta is colatitude measured from the north pole and phi longitude on the unit sphere; 'two-dimensional cylindrical coordinates' means plane polar (r, theta).
Phi(x, y, z) = -GM/r enters as g_tt = -(1 + 2 Phi) and, in the improved metric, g_ij = (1 - 2 Phi) delta_ij.
b closest approach to the Sun; d_p and d_e distances of planet and Earth along the x-axis from the point of closest approach; the signal runs from (-d_p, y0, z0) to (d_e, y0, z0).

margin_notes.summary: Epigraph: a boxing proverb about big fighters falling hard, attributed to two boxers of around 1900, as a pun on free fall.

Justifies geodesic motion: the free-particle action is minus mass times proper time, so stationary action means stationary proper time. Only free particles qualify, since other interactions add Lagrangian terms. Spacelike geodesics extremize proper length and are useful although nothing (except hypothetical tachyons) moves on them; photons use null geodesics.

General definition of a conjugate point as where the response matrix from initial-momentum to final-position variations fails to be invertible; a trajectory is a minimum if and only if it avoids conjugate points; two geodesics from P crossing again at Q make Q conjugate to P; points ahead to the singularity theorem of Chapter 50.
Chain-rule computation showing that the Cartesian length integral has identical form in any new parameter eta.
Remarks that the parameter effectively cancels from the Euler-Lagrange equation, which is why it can be chosen after taking derivatives.
Overdot means derivative with respect to the parameter lambda.
Gives the expanded form of the phi geodesic equation on the sphere, with the 2 cot theta thetadot phidot term.
Explicit tests: theta = lambda with phi = 0, and theta = pi/2 with phi = lambda, solve the sphere equations; theta = pi/4 with phi = lambda does not.

Any affine parameter linear in tau may replace tau, and affine parameters can be characterized as those keeping the geodesic equation in its standard form; photons have no proper time and obey the null condition with an affine parameter sigma.
For photons the momentum is tangent to the null world line, so nabla_p p = 0 also expresses momentum conservation for light.
Swingball is the British name for the game called tetherball elsewhere.
The method for obtaining the weak-field equation of motion is postponed to the next chapter.
Recalls the non-zero plane polar connection coefficients Gamma^theta_{r theta} = 1/r and Gamma^r_{theta theta} = -r.
Boxed contrast: free massive particles follow timelike geodesics while photons follow null geodesics; the former statement is called the geodesic principle.
The improved weak-field metric is derived in Section 14.1, with a fuller treatment in Chapter 45.

Irwin Shapiro proposed the time delay as a fourth test; the three classical solar-system tests are Mercury's perihelion precession and light deflection (Chapter 23) and gravitational redshift (Chapter 13).
With c restored the expansion parameter is GM/(c^2 r).
Supplies the standard integral of 1/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) needed for the delay.

notable.summary: Starting from the flat-space length written in polar coordinates, obtain the two geodesic equations and integrate them with length parametrization to get r^2 = lambda^2 + a^2, the angular rate a/(lambda^2 + a^2), and finally a tan(theta - theta0) = lambda.
notable.why_notable: Shows that a geodesic in curvilinear coordinates can look complicated even though it is a straight line, and practises the full solve-with-constraint workflow.

notable.summary: Eliminate the parameter from the previous solution to get r = a / cos(theta - theta0), then use Fig. 8.7 and given substitutions to confirm it is the Cartesian line alpha x + beta y = gamma.
notable.why_notable: Closes the loop between formalism and picture: the perpendicular distance a and direction theta0 are the natural line parameters.

notable.summary: Assume only that a particle has zero acceleration in coordinates moving with it, transform to arbitrary coordinates with the chain rule, derive an equation with a term built from second derivatives of the coordinate map, and interpret it.
notable.why_notable: Gives an independent, physics-first derivation of the geodesic equation and an explicit formula for Gamma in terms of the transformation to a freely falling frame, as in Weinberg's approach.

notable.summary: Given the covariant derivative of a 1-form, write the geodesic equation for the velocity 1-form (lower-index acceleration) and use it to show that the 4-force in the forced geodesic equation must be orthogonal to the 4-velocity.
notable.why_notable: Previews Part V machinery and establishes the physical constraint f.u = 0, which the chapter's force equation otherwise leaves implicit.

exercises.solutions: GA appE (Answers to selected problems, pdf p. 607, printed p. 590) sketches all four: 8.1 via the conserved r^2 thetadot = a combined with L = 1; 8.2(b) by substituting x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta; 8.3 by the chain rule, identifying Gamma^nu_{lambda sigma} = (partial x^nu / partial xi^mu)(partial^2 xi^mu / partial x^lambda partial x^sigma); 8.4 via the lower-index geodesic equation and differentiating u.u = -1.

difficulty.notes: The calculus of variations and index manipulations are standard for a second-year physics student, and every step of the plane and sphere calculations is shown. Harder are the conceptual points presented briefly: conjugate points and the second variation (only sketched with an unexplained response matrix), why the parameter may be fixed after differentiating, and the equivalence of the variational and parallel-transport definitions (not proven here). Several results are quoted rather than derived (the weak-field equation of motion, the improved metric 8.37), and there are printed or transcription slips (eqn 8.38, the cos theta in 8.17, index clashes) that can trip a careful reader. The Shapiro calculation is short but hides approximations (straight path, coordinate versus measured time).

teaching_gems.app_idea: Zigzag slider on a spacetime diagram with live clocks for the geodesic, a wavy path and its zigzag shadow.
